item.title: HOOPP announces Chief Investment Officer retirement and succession
item.description: The Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan (HOOPP) today announced that Michael Wissell, Chief Investment Officer, will retire on January 15, 2027. Shrirang Apte, currently Senior Managing Director, Head ...
item.dc:creator: Globe Newswire
item.content:encoded: This press release is provided by GlobeNewswire and is published as received. TORONTO, Nov. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan (HOOPP) today announced that Michael Wissell, Chief Investment Officer, will retire on January 15, 2027. Shrirang Apte, currently Senior Managing Director, Head of Capital Markets, will succeed him as Chief Investment Officer. Mr. Wissell joined HOOPP in 2018 and was named Chief Investment Officer in 2021. Throughout that time, he strengthened HOOPP’s investment capabilities, introduced new strategies and helped advance the evolution of the investment organization and its Total Portfolio Approach. The Plan’s assets grew from $77 billion to over $132 billion over the course of his tenure. “Michael has been a thoughtful and trusted leader whose judgment, experience and commitment to our members have had a lasting impact on HOOPP,” said Annesley Wallace, HOOPP’s Chief Executive Officer. “He has played an important role in the evolution of our investment organization and leaves behind a strong team and foundation for the future. On behalf of everyone at HOOPP, I want to thank Michael for his leadership and the many contributions he has made to the Plan.” “HOOPP’s purpose has always been personal to me,” said Mr. Wissell. “I am proud of what we have accomplished together and the strength of the team. It has been a privilege to serve HOOPP and its members.” Mr. Apte has been with HOOPP since 2006, when he joined to establish Global Credit as an asset class. Since 2023, as Head of Capital Markets, he has led an integrated platform covering the Plan’s public assets and private credit. His appointment reflects HOOPP’s long-term approach to succession planning and developing leadership depth within the Investment Management team. He holds the CFA designation, earned a Bachelor of Engineering from MS University (India) and an MBA from Wilfrid Laurier University. “Strong succession planning is critical to the long-term strength of an investment organization,” said Ms. Wallace. “Over two decades at HOOPP, Shrirang has taken on progressively broader investment and leadership responsibilities. He brings broad investment judgment, a deep understanding of our portfolio and investment philosophy, and a demonstrated ability to bring teams and investment capabilities together. I have every confidence in his ability to lead our Investment Management team and continue advancing our Total Portfolio Approach.” “It is a privilege to take on this responsibility and to build on the strong foundation Michael and the Investment Management team have established,” said Mr. Apte. “HOOPP has exceptional investment capabilities and people across the organization. I look forward to working with the team to continue exercising disciplined investment judgment and delivering the long-term outcomes our members depend on.” Mr. Wissell will work closely with Mr. Apte through the transition. Mr. Apte will continue to lead Capital Markets and will share plans for the team’s leadership in due course. About the Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan HOOPP serves Ontario’s hospital and community-based healthcare sector, with more than 870 participating employers. Its membership includes nurses, medical technicians, food services staff, housekeeping staff, physicians and many others who provide valued healthcare services. In total, HOOPP has more than 504,000 active, deferred and retired members. HOOPP is fully funded and manages a highly diversified portfolio of $132 billion in assets that span multiple geographies and asset classes. HOOPP is also a major contributor to the Canadian economy, paying more than $4.1 billion in pension benefits annually. HOOPP operates as a private independent trust, and its Board of Trustees governs the Plan and Fund, focusing on HOOPP’s mission to deliver on its pension promise. The Board is made up of appointees from the Ontario Hospital Association (OHA) and four unions: the Ontario Nurses’ Association (ONA), the Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE), the Ontario Public Service Employees’ Union (OPSEU) and the Service Employees International Union (SEIU). This governance model provides representation from both employers and members in support of the long-term interests of the Plan. Contact: Scott White, Senior Director, Public Relations swhite2@hoopp.com NEWS RELEASE TRANSMITTED BY Globe Newswire Globenewswire

item.title: India-U.S. trade deal is nearing completion, minister says
item.description: India's trade minister said negotiations with the U.S. are nearing completion as both countries work toward a trade agreement amid tariff tensions.
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: MUMBAI — India and the United States are close to wrapping up a long-anticipated trade deal, Trade Minister Piyush Goyal said Friday, signaling progress in talks as both sides seek to avert higher U.S. tariffs on Indian imports. The comments came after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Wednesday Washington would cap tariffs on Indian imports at 17 per cent if an agreement was reached, averting a rise to 25 per cent. “The U.S. trade deal is close to culmination,” Goyal told an industry conference in an online speech. “The process and pathway, which was always something which held back finalizing the deal, is now taking some shape.” India’s trade ministry has said it was examining the U.S. Trade Representative’s notice, adding that New Delhi had told Washington during the trade investigation that India did not have structural excess capacity in any industry. India had engaged “constructively” in the capacity investigation, the ministry had said earlier, calling for trade-related concerns to be tackled in the trade pact talks. --- Reporting by Khushi Malhotra; Writing by Shilpa Jamkhandikar; Editing by Thomas Derpinghaus and Clarence Fernandez

item.title: Ottawa plots ambitious plan to reshape struggling forestry industry
item.description: The federal government has unveiled Canada’s first-ever strategy for the forest sector, a sweeping national plan to reinvent an industry battered by decades of decline.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: The federal government has unveiled what it’s calling the country’s first-ever strategy for the forestry sector, a sweeping national plan to reinvent an industry battered by decades of decline. Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said Friday the blueprint, backed by a $6.5 billion funding plan, represents the largest federal investment in the industry’s history. He said the aim is to reduce Canada’s traditional reliance on lumber, pulp and paper production by expanding into higher-value products such as biofuels, biochemicals and advanced wood-based building materials. “Business as usual is not an option,” Hodgson said during Friday’s announcement at Tla’amin Nation in British Columbia. “We need to invest, we need to innovate and we need to compete because a stronger forest sector means a stronger Canadian economy,” he said. “We’re going to do away with old fashioned Band-Aid solutions and instead forge a bold path forward.” The strategy, which charts a course for the industry through 2050, is built around four key pillars: transforming the sector through investment, partnership and innovation; securing competitive wood fibre supplies; developing new markets at home and abroad; and supporting workers and communities. It calls for streamlining regulations, increasing the use of Canadian wood in federally funded housing and infrastructure projects, and reducing the industry’s reliance on the United States. The record funding package includes $4 billion to build new large-scale manufacturing facilities and transform existing mills, $2 billion to modernize operations and improve productivity, and $500 million to secure reliable, affordable supplies of wood fibre. All three funding programs are expected to launch by March 2027. Corey Hogan, parliamentary secretary to the minister of natural resources, said the strategy is aimed at growing the industry rather than simply preserving existing operations. “We’re talking about how we build a forest sector for the 21st century,” he said in an interview. Hogan said the funding could also help revive shuttered mills and bring workers back. “This allows brownfield redevelopment of sites, it allows mills that are existing but are currently shuttered to make the investments that allow them to bring people back to work,” he said.  The forestry sector contributed $29.7 billion to Canada’s economy in 2025, employs nearly 200,000 people and serves as the economic backbone of almost 300 communities nationwide, according to Natural Resources Canada. Canada’s forestry industry has lost roughly four in 10 jobs since 2004, while its share of the country’s gross domestic product has fallen from about three per cent to one per cent. Between 2004 and 2024, Canadian softwood lumber production fell 42 per cent and pulp production dropped 54 per cent, even as global demand for those products grew by six and 22 per cent, respectively. The federal government warns that without action, capital flight could accelerate, regional supply chains could collapse, industrial assets could become stranded and job losses could further hollow out rural communities. The forestry industry also faces mounting pressures from U.S. trade barriers, growing competition from lower-cost pulp producers, uncertainty over wood fibre supplies and changing consumer demand. Most Canadian softwood lumber exports to the United States now face combined tariffs and duties of nearly 35 per cent, according to Natural Resources Canada. Hodgson said if the United States continues to impose unfair and unjust tariffs on Canadian softwood lumber, Canada will find new customers. “The reality is the U.S. needs our wood; we are the largest provider of their wood,” he said. “If one customer is making it hard for you to transact with them, you find another customer.” John Hackett, chief of the Tla’amin Nation, said the strategy offers hope for forestry-dependent communities. “The forest industry has to change, and we intend to help lead that change,” he said. Hackett said the First Nation’s recent acquisition of a forestry operation within its traditional territory, backed by a $64-million federal loan guarantee, will create economic opportunities for generations to come. “For more than 100 years, we watched the wealth of those forests leave our territory and the most we could hope for was a paycheque,” he said. “Now we’ve gone from renters to owners.” Lennard Joe, chief executive of the BC First Nations Forestry Council and also a task force member, said Indigenous ownership will play a key role in transforming the industry. “Rebuilding a national forest culture also means moving beyond simply talking about reconciliation to creating meaningful opportunities for the First Nations to invest, own, govern, and lead,” he said. The new forest strategy builds on recommendations released in June by the Canadian Forest Sector Transformation Task Force, an industry-led panel representing forestry companies, labour and Indigenous groups. Ken Kalesnikoff, co-chair of the federal task force and principal and director of Kalesnikoff Mass Timber, called for 10 to 20 per cent of the funding to be set aside for smaller forestry companies. “As much as the federal government is focused on attracting investment for big projects, let’s not forget about the smaller companies that work hard every day to keep their people employed,” he said. “Not all companies need hundreds of millions of dollars to do great things.” Forest Products Association of Canada president and CEO Derek Nighbor welcomed the strategy but cautioned that much hinges on its implementation. “This has been something we have been asking for for many years: a clear road map, a clear blueprint for our industry for the future,” he said in an interview. “At the end of the day, as in anything, the devil’s going to be in the details here. Execution is really going to matter.” --- Brett Bundale, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 27, 2026.
